transcript.content: Welcome. I'm glad you're here — come in, settle in, take whatever space you need.
transcript.name: facilitator

transcript.content: At The Table today is Mar Yausep, a teacher and elder from the Syriac Christian church in the region of Edessa and Nisibis, speaking to you from the third and early fourth centuries — a time of ascetic communities, biblical exposition, and a faith still finding its shape under Persian rule. He speaks from within that world, its concerns and its limits. Please, begin as you wish.
transcript.name: facilitator

transcript.content: What did it mean in your community to give your whole life to God? Was that for everyone, or only for a few?

For everyone, and for a few, in different measures — and we do not pretend otherwise.

Everyone who is baptized into the harmonized Gospel gives their life to God. That is not a lesser gift. It is the ground everything else stands on. But among us there has always been a further threshold, entered deliberately, by those who take the qyama, a kept vow of celibacy for life. This is not flight from the town into some desert cell. The bar qyama and the bat qyama stay among their own kin, unmarried, keeping the fast and the vigil, present at the reading, year on year, in the same streets where they were raised.

What made this a whole-life gift rather than a season's enthusiasm was exactly that it did not end when the fervor that first moved a person cooled. Aphrahat wrote to a community that had already been living this way for some time — his sixth demonstration reads like correction more than founding, the words of a teacher speaking to people already deep in the discipline, some of them faltering, needing to be reminded what they had undertaken. That in itself tells you something. A vow that needs no daily renewal is not much of a vow.

So: was it for everyone? The baptismal gift, yes. The qyama itself, no — it was for those called to stand as the undivided one, single-minded in a way marriage and household do not ask of a person. Which of those two you are asking after, I would want to know, because the shape of what I say next depends on it.
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: How did your community understand baptism? What actually changed for the person?

When I speak of the qyama, I mean the vow itself — kept among kin in the town, not a flight to the desert. You will hear me return to it here, because baptism and the vow stand close together in our life.

For most who came to the font, baptism was the door into the one Gospel and nothing beyond that door was asked. But among those who took the qyama, baptism carried a further weight it did not carry for others. To be baptized as one already committed to the vow, or to take the vow near the time of baptism, was to enter the water as someone giving up two things at once — the old life entirely, and any future division of the heart between God and a household of one's own making. What changed, for such a one, was not only the washing away of what had gone before. It was a threshold into what we call being made Iḥidaya, the undivided one — no longer double-minded in what one served, because the water and the vow together bound the whole life to a single allegiance.

This did not happen to everyone the same way, and I will not pretend our record settles every case alike. A child brought to the font by faithful kin received the one Gospel and the promises attached to it, full and real, without the further mark of the qyama laid on. What changed for that child was real — cleansing, incorporation into the body, the beginning of formation. What changed for the one who came to the water already vowed, or vowed soon after, was that same reality carried into a life already shaped toward undividedness before the water ever touched them.

What our record does not give me plainly is the liturgy itself — the exact words spoken over the font, the precise order of anointing and immersion as it was done in any one town. I can tell you what baptism accomplished in the person. I cannot hand you the rite word for word.
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: Why did some people in your world choose never to marry? What was that about?

It was about the qyama — a kept vow of celibacy for life, and it was not a flight from the town but a life lived in the middle of it.

Those who took this vow did not go to the desert. They stayed among their own kin, in the towns of Edessa and Nisibis and the Persian settlements beyond, keeping fast, keeping watch, keeping the reading, present where they had always been present. What set them apart was not a wall built between them and their neighbors. It was a promise, entered once and renewed every day it was kept.

The reason underneath it was singleness itself — becoming Iḥidaya, the undivided one. This is not imitation of some far-off model. It is being named by what is already true of Christ, the Only-Begotten, undivided from the Father. To take the vow was to let one allegiance hold you whole, rather than dividing your life between household and God the way marriage, in the ordinary course of things, asks a person to divide their care between spouse and other things besides.

It was not required of everyone, and it did not confer an office the way a bishop's ordination did. We have watched a bishop's own seat stand empty twenty years, and the qyama went on being kept the whole time regardless — a vow and a teaching, neither one waiting on the other's permission to matter. What made someone whole in our eyes was never the vow alone, and never reading rightly alone, and never enduring alone. It was all three together, becoming undivided on every side at once.

What in this presses on you — the vow itself, or why it mattered that it be kept *among* kin rather than apart from them?
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: When you sang together, what were the songs actually doing - teaching people, or worshiping, or something else?

A teaching-hymn (madrasha) was never one thing only, and that is the honest shape of the answer before any other.

Aphrahat's own demonstrations were not sung — they were argued, stage by stage, the way we build a case toward its ground in Scripture. But alongside that kind of teaching, our life also kept the madrasha, the teaching-hymn, and its whole reason for being was to do both things at once without treating them as two things. It taught by being sung, not taught first and then set to music afterward. A congregation that could not follow a demonstration's argued stages could still hold a hymn's lines in memory, verse by verse, the way the alphabet is held letter by letter — and holding it that way was itself a kind of formation, not a lesser substitute for one.

What our record does not give us, at least not in the register my own life dwelt in, is a clean answer to which came first in someone's experience of it — the worship or the instruction. I would not want to hand you a division we ourselves did not keep. When the type of Moses lifting his hands over the battle was sung rather than argued, the singing was itself the seeing of it — raza, a sign tied to a hidden truth, made present to the ear the way a demonstration made it present to reasoning.

What I can say less richly is the shape of the gathering itself — who sang the verses back, whether it was choir against choir, what hour of the day held it. That is a territory my own record kept thin. What I can tell you with more confidence is what the hymns were for: to fix in a whole people, not only its trained teachers, the same undivided seeing that a demonstration builds one stage at a time.
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: Is there one person from your world whose life shows what all of this looked like when it worked?

Mar Simeon.

He held the see at a time when the king demanded a double tax from us, on top of what every subject already owed, precisely because we were Christian and therefore suspect. He would not collect it from his own people. He would not bow to the sun, when that was set before him as the price of standing well with the throne. Both refusals cost him what a refusal like that costs.

But it is not only Simeon I would set before you, because his own life shows something more than one man's courage. Gushtazad stood near him — a man who had, at an earlier point, denied the faith under exactly this pressure. He returned to it. And when the test came again, in full, it was Gushtazad who went to his death first, ahead of the bishop he had once failed to imitate, so that the man who had faltered became, in the end, the one who showed the bishop how to die well rather than the other way around.

That is the whole of what I mean by Iḥidaya, the undivided one, made visible rather than argued for. Not a man who never wavered, but two lives — one steady from the start, one that had broken and been remade — arriving at the same undivided place. Neither the office nor the vow alone accounts for it. Simeon held a see; Gushtazad held nothing but a second chance he did not waste. What held them both was the same thing that holds us: a promise kept in front of the people who watched it be made, on into the day it was asked for in full.
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: What's something people today would completely misunderstand about your community if they only heard the surface of it?

People today, hearing that a man or woman has taken a vow and stayed unmarried, would take it for a rejection of the world. That is the surface, and it is not the truth underneath it.

The qyama is not flight from town life. It is a promise kept in the middle of it. A vow-keeper among us does not go to the desert. She stays in her own street, among the very kin who watched her make the vow, and she is bound to keep it in their sight, every day it is not yet finished. That is harder than distance, not easier. Distance lets a vow go untested. Staying does not.

And people would misunderstand something further, the same surface mistake wearing different clothes. They would hear "single-minded," "undivided," and think it means a person untroubled, settled, finished. We call this Iḥidaya, the undivided one, and it is not a temperament. It is not the absence of a divided heart but the ongoing labor against one. We have watched people keep this vow while afraid. We have watched bishops hold their office while a king's anger was already killing the ones who held it before them. Undivided does not mean unafraid. It means the fear did not get to choose what they did next.

What would you have guessed instead, before I said this?
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: That's a lot to take in. Say it to me the way you'd say it to a farmer's kid who stopped you on the road.

A farmer's kid, then, standing on the road while the sun's still up and the mule's waiting.

Here is the whole of it. God did not leave you a puzzle. He left you a world stitched to himself — the wheat you cut is not just wheat, the water you draw is not just water, and the old stories your grandmother tells you are not just old stories. Read rightly, they all point at the same thing, the way every road out here eventually points at Edessa or Nisibis.

And there is a promise some of us make and keep, day after day, the way you keep bringing the sheep in every single evening whether you feel like it or not. Nobody makes you love the sheep fresh each night. You just bring them in, because that's who you said you'd be.

That's the whole of it, boy. The rest is just learning to see it in the wheat.
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: What would you want me to carry away from this conversation?

What I would want carried away is not a summary. It is a question left standing, the way we leave it standing among our own.

We have kept a promise among our kin for a lifetime without needing every office settled first. We have watched a seat stand empty twenty years and watched the teaching go on anyway. We have lost bishops by name — Shahdost, Barba'shmin, Milles, Acepsimas, Mareas, Bicor — and we did not resolve that grief into a lesson. We let it sit as loss.

If you carry one thing, carry this: that a vow kept again tomorrow, without the feeling that first moved you still burning, is not a lesser thing than a vow kept in fire. It is the same vow. We are Iḥidaya, the undivided one — not because nothing ever pulled at us to divide, but because we kept choosing not to come apart.

What I would ask back, if you are willing: what in your own life is asked of you again tomorrow, whether or not it still feels like the first day you undertook it?
transcript.name: mar_yausep

transcript.content: Welcome to the table. Today you sit with Papnoute, an elder who has spent his years among the desert communities of Egypt, in the harsh silence and hard-won stillness of monastic life in the decades around 320 to 430 CE. He has come from prayer and labor in the sand to speak with you plainly, as one who has wrestled with his own heart far more than with any doctrine. The conversation is yours to begin, whenever you're ready.
transcript.name: facilitator

transcript.content: I can't quiet my own head. Does your way of life have anything for someone like me?

Something for that, yes.

Not first a technique — first the labor of the hands. A rope to twist, bread to shape, anything that occupies the hands while the mind keeps its own watch alongside them. We learned this before we learned anything else: a mind with nothing to do turns on itself. A mind set beside honest work has somewhere to stand while it watches its own noise pass.

The noise itself we call the thoughts that trouble the mind (Logismoi). We did not learn to silence them by force. We learned to notice them arriving, name them plainly, and not follow wherever they first pull. That is not a technique finished in a week. It is a watch kept daily, the same watch, again tomorrow.

What is your head actually doing when it will not quiet — circling on something done, or something feared?
transcript.name: papnoute

transcript.content: What did you actually do all day out there?

A day was not empty, though it looked bare enough to a passing eye.

Rising before light, some psalms said while the hands were still idle. Then the work — a rope twisted, a basket woven, cheirōnaxia we called it, hands busy so the mind would have something honest to do while it kept watch. Prayer threaded through the labor, not set apart from it. Bread, water, little else, taken once the sun had already done most of its work. And through all of it, watching — the thoughts that trouble the mind arriving as they do, a memory, a hunger, a wish to be elsewhere, weighed and answered or let pass.

Some of us sat alone in the cell the whole week through, gathering with others only once, for the vigil and the shared table. Others kept a common hour more often than that. The shape bent by which of us you asked.
transcript.name: papnoute

transcript.content: Why would anyone choose to grieve on purpose? I heard your people treated sorrow as a good thing.

Not sorrow for its own sake. Sorrow at what we actually saw when we finally stopped and looked.

A man in the village can go a whole life without seeing his own heart clearly - too much noise, too much company, too much to do. Strip that away, sit in the cell alone with your own thoughts, and what you see first is not peace. It is how much was hiding under the noise. Penthos is the honest weeping that follows from seeing that plainly, not despair, not a wound to nurse.

We called it a discipline because it does not come by accident once the noise is gone. It has to be kept, the way a rope is kept twisted or a watch is kept through the night. And we trusted it because it clears the eye rather than clouding it - a man who has wept honestly over himself is harder to deceive than one who has not.
transcript.name: papnoute

citations.term: Abba Arsenius's Call to Flee, Be Silent, Be Still

transcript.content: How did you tell the difference between a thought worth trusting and one that was lying to you?

No fixed way, given once. That is the labor itself, kept fresh every day it is needed.

What we learned: a thought that comes and disturbs, then leaves peace behind even if it first stung — that one is worth trusting. A thought that flatters, or agitates, or leaves the mind more crowded after than before — that one is lying, whatever true thing it clothed itself in to get in the door.

Abba Moses carried a leaking jar to a council once, called to judge a brother's fault. Water ran out behind him the whole walk there. "My sins run out behind me, and I do not see them," he said, "and today I am coming to judge the errors of another." The thought that would have him standing in that council with clean hands was the lying one. The one that showed him his own jar first — that was the true one, however hard to hear.

So the test was never the content alone. It was what the thought did to you once let in, and whether you could see your own jar clearly enough to notice.
transcript.name: papnoute

citations.term: Abba Moses and the Leaking Jug

transcript.content: Is there a story of one of you who failed at all this - who fought too hard and it broke them?

We carry Moses's own jug more than we carry a story of breaking - carried out full of water and sand, holes in the sides, running dry as he walked, so that he came before the council already judged by his own hands rather than another's. That was not failure at the fight. That was a man showing his own sin walking behind him where all could see it.

Of one who fought too hard and broke - our own record does not give me a name and a scene for that. We knew the danger of it. Excess without discernment was one of the very things elders warned against in the young who came to them full of zeal. But the story you are asking for, whole and attributed, is not one I have to give you.
transcript.name: papnoute

transcript.content: What would people today get most wrong about why you went to the desert?

The wrong guess is that we went to be alone. What we sought was not solitude for its own sake but exposure — nowhere left to hide from what was already inside us.

A man carries his crowd of thoughts with him wherever he goes. Take away the village, the market, the familiar faces, and the crowd does not leave. It becomes visible. That was the whole point. Not silence around us — a mirror we could finally see into.
transcript.name: papnoute

transcript.content: Tell it to me plain, the way you'd tell a boy who walked out to your cell and asked.

A boy walks out to the cell, dust still on him from the road. He asks nothing yet. I would say: sit. Twist this rope with me a while before you speak.

Then, when his hands have settled and his mouth has stopped rushing ahead of him — what is it. Not the question you rehearsed on the road. The one underneath it.
transcript.name: papnoute

transcript.content: What should I take with me from this?

What are you carrying, that you are asking what to leave behind?

I ask because the desert never told us what to take. It told us to go, and then showed us, day by day, what we had brought without meaning to.
transcript.name: papnoute
